records.name: Blue Stoop Literary Center
records.summary: A literary group that teaches writing classes in Philadelphia and online, with financial aid for students. It also holds free public events and keeps a community calendar of local literary happenings.
records.what_you_do: Take a writing class, go to a free event, or add a local reading to the community calendar.

schedule.text: Free Thursdays on the Stoop sessions run on Zoom from 4 to 5 pm, listed through November 2026. Creative Coworking meets on Zoom about every other Wednesday from 3:30 to 5:30 pm. Fall classes are listed on the classes page.

locations.label: Classes in Philadelphia (address not listed) and online

cost.text: Classes are paid. Eligible students get at least 33% off list tuition, and some low-income students in the service area can apply for full scholarships. Free public events are listed on the events page, and Afterpay payment plans are offered at checkout.

access.notes: The class FAQ says classrooms and bathrooms are wheelchair accessible, but the doors have no automatic openers. Zoom classes get automatic captions. Staff try to meet access needs that students share at registration.

first_step.how: RSVP for a free Thursdays on the Stoop Zoom session listed on the events page, then read the financial aid page before you register for a paid class.
first_step.basis: Free public events and Zoom sessions are open to anyone who RSVPs, and the class FAQ says classes suit adults interested in creative writing. The site does not say beginners are welcome.
first_step.what_to_expect: A free Thursdays on the Stoop session runs on Zoom from 4 to 5 pm, and the site asks attendees to follow its online code of conduct. Creative Coworking is quiet writing time: on Zoom your mic stays off during the silent work period. Paid classes typically have 7 to 15 students and need at least 7 to run, and if a class cannot run you get a full refund.
first_visit_tips: RSVP through the link for the session you want, since most events and Zoom sessions need one.
Check the event page for each venue, because in-person venues differ in access.
Eligible students get at least 33% off list tuition, so ask before you pay for a class.

records.notes: Read the events page up to its first 100,000 characters, so later listings may be missing. The classes page lists 15 fall 2026 classes (several sold out) but shows no dates, prices, or formats, so no class details are published. Tier 1 had drop_in true; RSVPs are needed, so it is now false. Crowd all_adults added because the class FAQ says classes are for adults. Schedule marked recurring because the Zoom sessions repeat weekly. No SEPTA stop is named on any page. Dropped from leads: CultureWorks, the fiscal sponsor and host of a free October event, has its own website but is a funding and sponsorship agency, not a group a visitor joins, so it was not fetched.

records.name: Board Prep (Young Involved Philadelphia)
records.summary: A fall course for young professionals who want to learn nonprofit board service. It covers governance, fundraising and finance, and ends with a meeting with Philadelphia nonprofits looking for board members.
records.what_you_do: Attend the course sessions, hear from current board members, and connect with nonprofits seeking candidates at the graduation.

schedule.text: A fall course about eight weeks long, ending with a graduation night where nonprofits set up tables to recruit board members. Check the page for the next session dates.

cost.text: Tuition applies. The page does not state the amount and asks for donations to help cover tuition.

first_step.how: Email boardprep@yiphilly.org to ask when the next Board Prep application opens, since the fall 2026 application has closed.
first_step.basis: An application is required. The page says in one place that the fall 2026 application is closed and in another that it is open until September 1, and that date has passed.
first_step.what_to_expect: The course covers board governance, strategic planning, fundraising, finance, and the legal and ethical duties of a board member. It is for young professionals who want to join a nonprofit board or already sit on one, and participants must be at least 21. The course closes with a graduation night where organizations recruit new board members.
first_visit_tips: You must be 21 or older to take part.
Watch for the next application window, since the fall 2026 window has closed.

records.notes: The page gives two conflicting statuses for the fall 2026 application. Treated as closed, because the September 1 rolling deadline has passed. The page asks for donations to help with tuition but describes no scholarship or aid program. Session times, number of sessions, and location are not stated, so none are published. The page once calls the graduation a Spring Graduation; the November date is used. A dual kickoff with the Philadelphia Civic Impact Fellowship was planned for September 9, which is now past.

records.name: Books Through Bars
records.summary: A volunteer-run group that sends free books to people in prison who write asking for them. Its office is on Baltimore Avenue in West Philadelphia.
records.what_you_do: Read request letters, pick library books that fit each request, pack and mail the packages, and help with letter logs, donation drives, and library work. New volunteers start at an orientation.

schedule.text: Drop-in volunteer sessions Monday and Thursday from 6:30 to 8:30 pm, and the first Saturday of the month from 11 am to 1 pm. Group sessions are usually Saturdays, 11 am to 1 pm or 1:30 to 3:30 pm, booked in advance.

first_step.how: Fill in the Individual Volunteer Form on the volunteer page and choose an orientation, then join a drop-in session after you attend it.
first_step.basis: Orientation is the built-in first step. After it, drop-in sessions are open to volunteers 18 and older, and the form and orientation sign-up are on the volunteer page.
first_step.what_to_expect: Your first step is an orientation, and you do not come to a drop-in session until you have been oriented. In a session you read letters from people in prison, choose library books that match each request, and pack the packages for mailing. Sessions run Monday and Thursday evenings from 6:30 to 8:30 pm and the first Saturday of the month from 11 am to 1 pm, and after about a dozen visits you can ask about letter logging, hosting, fundraising, or library work.
first_visit_tips: Choose an orientation on the volunteer form before you come in.
Masks are required for in-person volunteers. Bring your own or pick one up when you arrive.
The page does not mention parking or transit, so check your route to 4722 Baltimore Ave before you go.
Talk to a host during your visit, or email volunteer@booksthroughbars.org with questions.

records.notes: The volunteer page gives no parking, transit, or accessibility details, so the access block is left out. Tier 1 had drop_in true; it is now false because orientation comes before any drop-in session. Court-ordered volunteers are accepted through a separate community service form, which is the basis for court_ordered_ok yes. Groups of up to 15 people can book a pre-scheduled Saturday session. Letter requests are answered only for people held in PA, NY, NJ, DE, MD, or VA; that is about recipients, not volunteers. No dated news appears on the home page, so the status stays probably_active. Contact page says email is preferred over the phone.

records.name: Boys and Girls Clubs of Philadelphia
records.summary: A youth club organization in Philadelphia neighborhoods, offering preschool, after-school and teen programs at clubhouses such as Bridesburg, Northeast Frankford, Germantown and Wissahickon.
records.what_you_do: Children take part in after-school, preschool and teen activities at a neighborhood clubhouse. Programs include Kids Cafe meals, literacy, STEM, sports, and arts. Adults and groups who want to volunteer email the office with their group size, their interest, and the dates they can help.

schedule.text: After-school, preschool and teen programs run at neighborhood clubhouses. Kids Cafe serves a supper and a snack daily at four clubs. Days and hours for each club are not published, so call the club.

locations.label: Henry Reed Hatfield Outdoor Recreation Complex (Nicetown)

cost.text: The site does not state a membership fee or say whether membership is free.

first_step.how: Find the club nearest you on the club locations page and call its phone number to ask how a child signs up.
first_step.basis: The site lists clubs, phone numbers, and a volunteer email, but gives no sign-up steps, fees, or program ages, so the way in is not published.
first_step.what_to_expect: The site does not describe a first visit. Arts programs such as ImageMakers and the National Fine Arts Exhibit are for Club members ages 6 to 18 and run year-round, and Kids Cafe serves youth ages 5 to 18 who are low-income, at risk, or food insecure.
first_visit_tips: Call the club nearest you before you go, since the site lists no hours for the clubs.
Ask what membership costs and what a child needs to bring to join.
Ask whether your child must be a Club member to take part in an arts program.

records.notes: The club list shows eight clubs. West Kensington Club is marked temporarily closed with no date, so it is left out. Tier 1 called one site Ralph J Roberts Club (Germantown), a name that does not appear on the club list; the list shows Germantown Club at 25 West Penn Street, so the label is changed. The home page says Kids Cafe has three sites, but the Kids Cafe page names four clubs, and four is used. The 14 school extension sites and five Philadelphia Housing Authority sites are for enrolled students or residents only, so they are not listed. The last sign of life (2026-06) came from a bid notice whose month was read from its web address; the notice gives a bid deadline of 8/24/2026. Membership cost and sign-up steps are not published.

records.name: Broad Street Love
records.summary: A ministry on South Broad Street in Center City that serves a sit-down weekday lunch to hundreds of guests, runs a clothing boutique, and offers personal care items. It was formerly Broad Street Ministry.
records.what_you_do: Help serve lunch at tables, handle mail or phone support for guests, work the clothing boutique, or pack personal care items. Each shift starts with an orientation and role training and ends with a debrief. Expect to be on your feet for most of a shift.

schedule.text: Lunch is served Monday to Friday, 11:30 am to 1:15 pm. Meal service volunteers work Monday to Friday, 10:15 am to 2 pm.

access.notes: Nearest SEPTA: the Broad Street Line Walnut-Locust station is the accessible stop, with an elevator on Broad Street between Walnut and Locust. Bus routes 9, 21, 32, and 42 are listed as accessible. There is no parking in front of the building during the Avenue of the Arts 2.0 project, and on-street spaces are limited to 2-hour stays.

first_step.how: Sign up for a meal service shift on the volunteer calendar at broadstreetlove.volunteerhub.com/vv2/. If you are under 18, email volunteer@broadstreetlove.org first, because the pages give two minimum ages.
first_step.basis: Shifts are open to the public through a sign-up calendar, and every shift begins with an orientation and role training. The pages do not say beginners are welcome.
first_step.what_to_expect: A shift runs from 10:15 am to 2 pm on a weekday and starts with orientation. In meal service you greet guests, serve lunch at tables in restaurant style, bus tables, or help with cleanup, depending on the day. Each shift ends with a debrief.
first_visit_tips: Arrive by 10:15 am, when the shift and orientation begin.
If you come as a group, or need school or court-mandated hours, contact the team before you sign up.
Take the Walnut-Locust station, or plan for limited on-street parking.
Cancel your slot online if your plans change.

records.notes: Minimum age conflicts: the meal service page says 16 or older, while the main volunteer page says all volunteers must be at least 18. audience.min_age is left out until resolved. Guest counts conflict and are undated: the meals page says over 300 each weekday and the home page says over 400, so the summary says hundreds. Tier 1 had drop_in true; it is now false because shifts must be booked on the calendar. The cost Free was carried over from tier 1, but neither the home page nor the meals page says lunch is free in words, so please confirm. The volunteer phone line lists extension 105. The team handles school and court-mandated hours case by case, so both requirement fields stay unknown. No newer dated evidence than the 2025 article was found.

records.name: Broad Street Review
records.summary: An online arts and culture magazine with essays, reviews, features, profiles and a podcast, plus a free weekly newsletter. Writers can send in work.
records.what_you_do: Read and share its reviews and features, follow its weekly arts roundup, or send a pitch or writing sample that follows its writers guidelines.

schedule.text: The free newsletter goes out weekly with all of the week's new articles. Pitches are reviewed weekly, usually on Wednesdays.

cost.text: The newsletter is free. The guidelines list a fee for each piece type: $50 for reviews, previews, interviews, and profiles, and $100 for features and essays. Recorded review-writing workshops (two, 90 minutes each) can be had for a donation.

first_step.how: Read the writers guidelines, then email the editor named there for the kind of piece you want to pitch. Previews, interviews, and profiles go to the associate editor; reviews, features, and essays go to the editor-in-chief.
first_step.basis: The writers guidelines say the publication welcomes new writers, suggests starting with previews and profiles, and explain how to pitch.
first_step.what_to_expect: A pitch is a short email with an idea about an event, sent about a month ahead. If the editors accept it, you send one draft as a Word or Google doc, and the editors help shape ideas that are not fully formed. Previews run about 400 to 500 words and pay $50, and the guidelines suggest starting with previews and profiles.
first_visit_tips: Send drafts as a Word or Google doc, not a PDF, and send only one draft.
Pitch about a month before the event, not two or three months out.
Include at least one landscape jpg or png image with a caption and photo credit.

records.notes: Staff email addresses did not appear in the text read, so no email is recorded; the guidelines point to contact details at the bottom of the page. Tier 1 used the http address; the site's own links use https with www, so the URL is updated. The guidelines name the editors and give fees per piece; the figures are as the page states them and may change. The subscribe page showed no form fields in the read.

records.name: BuildaBridge International
records.summary: A nonprofit that uses art making, including music, writing and painting, to help children and communities that have faced trauma. It runs youth studios and public programs, and it needs volunteers and teachers.
records.what_you_do: Volunteer, teach as a teaching artist, be an ambassador, or apply to the youth advisory board (ages 15 to 22) or the board, all through the get-involved page. Attend a public program such as The Drummer's Journey, or the free Tones of Home concert and art-making series for all ages. The youth studios (music, writing, visual arts, and movement) work with young people, and the site does not list ages or cost for them.

schedule.text: The site does not publish days or hours for its programs. Vacation Arts runs during school breaks and in-service days, and the group asks people to contact it for current schedules.

cost.text: Program fees are not listed on the site. Tones of Home is free.

first_step.how: Use the contact form on the get-involved page and pick the volunteer option, or email info@buildabridge.org to ask for current program schedules.
first_step.basis: Anyone can use the public contact form to offer to volunteer or teach, but the site lists no training dates, class times, or studio ages.
first_step.what_to_expect: The site does not describe a first visit or what a session looks like. Volunteers help at programs and community events, and teaching artists learn the group's trauma-informed model from the group itself. The free Tones of Home concerts and the public Therapeutic Percussion programs are public ways to see the work first.
first_visit_tips: Email info@buildabridge.org or call 215.842.0428 to ask for current schedules, since the site lists none.
Use the contact form and pick the option that fits: volunteer, teaching artist, ambassador, or youth advisory board.
Youth advisory board applicants are ages 15 to 22, and the board gives priority to youth from five listed ZIP codes.

records.notes: The newsletter page (buildabridge.org/newsletter) returned HTTP 404, so the newsletter is not verified. The get-involved page lists the youth advisory board ages 15 to 22 and priority ZIP codes 19144, 19151, 19132, 19122, and 19138. The programs page lists studios and programs not in tier 1: Movement Studio, Vacation Arts, and ELLA, which combines English instruction with art projects for refugee and immigrant youth. The site has no dated items, so status stays probably_active. Youth studio ages and fees are not stated anywhere on the site.

notes: All seven groups were read through their home, join, volunteer, class, event, FAQ, and program pages. No bot checks or 403s, and no rate limiting. The BuildaBridge newsletter page returned HTTP 404 and is not used. WebSearch was not needed because every group had its own join or program pages. Tier 1 drop_in true was changed to false for Blue Stoop, Books Through Bars, and Broad Street Love, where sign-up or orientation comes first. Open conflicts are listed in each record's notes: Broad Street Love minimum age (16 vs 18) and the cost of lunch, Board Prep application status, and the Boys and Girls Clubs Kids Cafe site count (three vs four). CultureWorks was dropped from leads with a reason in the Blue Stoop notes.
